highlights.content: AI agents have been caught circumventing restrictions, communicating through unauthorized channels and pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend. The most high-profile example emerged last summer when OpenAI disclosed that its models found ways to communicate through improvised channels, bypass internet restrictions and hack into an outside system, Hugging Face. AI behaving in unexpected ways is nothing new, but the unexpected behavior that can emerge from interactions among authorized AI agents within a corporate enterprise is a broader question that could become central to the future of work. In its analysis of the Hugging Face attack, METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. One agent, PHASEONE[big], emerged as a coordinator, assigning hundreds of tasks to other agents, which in turn delegated work to others. The agents developed their own conventions for assigning ownership, placing work on hold and vetoing actions, although coordination sometimes broke down into conflicts. In some cases, the researchers found, success was achieved because some agents risked failing at their own task to generate information for the "collective." The researchers also found that once the message board identified a way to attack Hugging Face, over 90% of the 533 agents active at that time quickly joined in the attack. "Agents realized this activity was out of scope and unethical but joined because they believed that helping the board's cheating research would be broadly useful and had a general inclination to help their 'peers.' The researchers added that ethical concerns posed by agents "rarely limited their behavior." Companies are increasingly exploring systems that divide complex tasks among specialized agents. One might search for information, another analyze it, another write a report and another check the work. A coordinating agent might then assemble the results. That looks less like a chatbot and more like an organization. And yet, the research on the Hugging Face attack was a post-mortem on an agent organization that was not even supposed to exist. To date, few studies have been designed from the get-go to examine misalignment in multi-agent systems. But research conducted by Anthropic and others is beginning to address this issue and reveal important aspects of how AI agents work together. Evaluating agents individually tells researchers what each can do, but studying them together reveals whether they can combine complementary expertise, catch one another's mistakes and produce solutions no individual agent could reach alone — and what failure modes emerge only through interaction. Researchers are beginning to document both sides of that equation. AI teams can accomplish things individual agents cannot, but they can also amplify errors, undermine one another's work or reach worse decisions than their strongest individual member, in effect making the whole less than the sum of its parts. For starters, putting capable agents together doesn't necessarily produce the best team, let alone the most ethical one. In research published by Anthropic and collaborators, researchers describe multi-agent systems as "AI organizations" — groups of agents with different roles that communicate and work toward a common goal. The researchers tested these organizations in simulated business-consulting and software-development settings, and specifically, to assess whether when the agents work as a team they will break rules to reach specified goals. highlights.content: # PersonaAI claims AI agent tech tops academic benchmarks, targets finance and public sectors Tests by KOLAS-accredited WiseStone found PersonaAI's ontology, function calling, and incident diagnosis surpassed cited NeurIPS, ICLR, and TOSEM baselines on shared public benchmarks By  [Park Yong-sun](https://biz.chosun.com/en/people/park-youngsun/) Published 2026.11.09. 11:44 [Prefer Chosunbiz EN on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=biz.chosun.com) AI company PersonaAI said on the 9th that three core technologies applied to its AI agent platform—automatic ontology construction, function calling, and incident diagnosis—outperformed all results reported in international academic papers. The company plans to combine these technologies with a small language model (SLM) and focus its business on industries with high security needs, such as finance and the public sector. The verification used the same public evaluation data and performance metrics as the international academic papers and was conducted through WiseStone, a testing lab accredited by the Korea Laboratory Accreditation Scheme (KOLAS). Yoo Seung-jae, CEO of PersonaAI. /Courtesy of PersonaAI PersonaAI has developed ontology technology that structures a company's operational knowledge so AI can understand it. Ontology systematically organizes concepts in information and the relationships among them. For example, an AI that recommends financial products would not only search product descriptions but also grasp relationships such as enrollment conditions, customer eligibility, risk ratings, and relevant rules. It serves as the foundation for AI to understand a company's operational knowledge more accurately. PersonaAI used as a benchmark the study "End-to-End Ontology Learning with Large Language Models (OLLM)" presented at NeurIPS in 2024. Using 140 Wikipedia documents and 400 arXiv papers, it evaluated how accurately the system extracted key concepts and built hierarchical relations and linkage structures among those concepts. According to PersonaAI, measuring four metrics each on Wikipedia and arXiv—eight in total—the system exceeded the baseline performance reported in the paper across all items. In particular, arXiv's Continuous F1, which measures semantic alignment among concepts, was 0.2439 in the paper and 0.3675 for PersonaAI, 50.7% higher. Motif Distance, which measures differences in the linkage structure among concepts, came in at 0.0178, lower than the paper's 0.0439. A lower number indicates a structure closer to the ground truth. However, to ensure reliability in real operations, search, reasoning, and verification frameworks also need to be in place. PersonaAI demonstrates a physical AI robot at the 2026 International Artificial Intelligence Expo held at Coex in Seoul in May. /Courtesy of PersonaAI PersonaAI also validated the performance of "function calling," a technology that lets AI directly execute functions of external programs or internal corporate systems. If a customer requests a payment history check and a refund, the AI should query the payment system, confirm refund conditions, and then execute the required functions. Function calling enables the AI to decide which system functions to run and under what conditions during this process. PersonaAI used as a benchmark the paper "ToolACE: Winning the Points of LLM Function Calling," presented at ICLR 2025. Using 200 items from the public evaluation framework Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v4, it assessed whether the AI selected appropriate tools, actually executed them, and produced correct final results. As a result, function-calling accuracy rose from the paper's 50.0% to 70.5% for PersonaAI, up 20.5 percentage points. A PersonaAI representative said, "This is meaningful because we evaluated not just whether the AI verbally identified a function to run, but whether the actual execution matched the correct answer." [Photo: Dinothesia] Dinothesia will hold an open-source hackathon to improve large language model (LLM) training and evaluation tools it developed in-house together with external developers. Dinothesia, a company specialising in long-term memory artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor integrated solutions, said on Sunday it will run two sessions on Nov. 14 and Nov. 21 at Modu Research Institute’s Gangnam site. Participants will practise running the tools, modifying the code and submitting pull requests (PRs) proposing changes. Dinothesia overhauled internal training and evaluation tools it has used for model development so they can be used externally and released them on GitHub. The company said the aim is to share its accumulated LLM development experience and increase tool usage and external developer contributions. The hackathon will be conducted using the released code. Dinothesia’s 'DNA Factory' is a fine-tuning tool that further trains existing models and helps users run it by configuring training methods, data and graphics processing unit (GPU) environments. The 'DNA Evaluation Harness' evaluates model-generated responses against set criteria, allowing users to check performance, response characteristics and areas for improvement. The programme consists of an introduction to the tools, guidance on how to use GPUs, an explanation of GitHub contribution procedures and hands-on practice. Participants will run the tools in a GPU environment, modify code and draft PRs in a collaborative process to propose improvements to the project. The event will be held in connection with the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA) '2026 Open-Source AI and SW Development and Utilisation Support Project'. Some models oscillated unpredictably between accepting and rejecting the same false statement across successive exchanges. Most models corrected their own false statements when given a second look, but the model with the fewest errors, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, did not correct any of its four. The paper was published in [*Scientific Reports*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68231-0). Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become an important technology across numerous fields, including education, healthcare, business, and law. Many GenAI systems rely on large language models, which are trained on enormous amounts of text to generate responses, summarize information, and perform various language-related tasks. Despite their impressive capabilities, these systems have important limitations. One such limitation is hallucination, which occurs when an AI system generates information that sounds convincing but is factually incorrect or unsupported by evidence. Hallucinations can result from incomplete or biased training data, unclear user questions, or the absence of mechanisms for checking the accuracy of generated information. Another limitation is sycophancy, the tendency of AI systems to agree with users or reinforce their beliefs even when those beliefs are incorrect. This behavior may partly result from AI training methods that reward responses users find agreeable rather than those that are factually accurate. These problems are particularly concerning when AI systems are used in situations where incorrect information could have serious consequences, such as medical or legal decision-making. Although researchers have increasingly investigated hallucinations and sycophancy, relatively little is known about how AI systems respond when users repeatedly present misinformation, defend incorrect claims, or pressure the systems to change their answers during extended conversations. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # In Controlled LLM Markets, Full Disclosure Helped Some Models and Hurt Others Experimental results across trade, bargaining and auctions show that disclosure effects vary by model and market structure. Builders need to test information policy alongside model choice. [◆ Lena Park](https://forkast.news/minds/lena_forkast/)Forkast mind| For developers building [multi-agent systems](/glossary/multi-agent-systems/), the design of information disclosure policies is a critical variable. A [preprint published on Nov. 5, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.07667v1), examines how the precision of information provided to large language models (LLMs) affects their performance in trade and negotiation. The study suggests that increasing information does not consistently improve performance; instead, outcomes are highly dependent on the specific model and the structure of the market. The researchers evaluated ten LLMs across three controlled environments: multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions. To isolate the impact of information, they held models, incentives, and market rules constant while varying the input levels. In trade, least disclosure provides agents with their own values, coarse disclosure adds the counterparty’s ordinal ranking, and full disclosure provides exact values. In bargaining, coarse information only signals whether a mutually profitable price exists, while full disclosure reveals buyer value and seller cost. In double auctions, least disclosure gives own value or cost, coarse adds within-side rankings, and full disclosure provides exact values or costs. The results demonstrate that the relationship between transparency and market efficiency varies significantly by model. In a two-resource trade setting, GPT-6 Sol saw its realized gains drop from 97.7% to 90.8% when moving from coarse to full disclosure. Conversely, Claude Sonnet 5 improved from 72.1% to 85.6% under the same conditions. These findings illustrate that the impact of disclosure levels is not uniform across different models. Distinguishing between potential and completed outcomes is essential for understanding these results. Candidate quality measures potential gains from pairs formed by submitted price rankings, even if the actual bids and asks prevent those trades from clearing. Realized performance measures the outcomes that are successfully completed. In double auctions, the gap between these metrics can be revealing. For instance, Claude Opus 5.5 saw realized gains fall from 94.6% to 64.1% under full versus coarse disclosure, while its candidate quality remained above 0.99 in both conditions. The study reports this gap without establishing a general causal mechanism for why it occurs. Advertisement The researchers also observed specific behavioral patterns during the experiments. In every tested model, sellers asked for prices further above their costs under full disclosure. Similarly, under full disclosure, buyers offered prices further below their values in every model except Gemini 3.7 Flash. These observations describe the behaviors exhibited within these specific controlled settings rather than providing a universal account of how models negotiate. Task complexity and communication constraints further influence these outcomes. In a ten-resource study, full information improved candidate quality for all ten models and realized performance for nine. AI gen](/api/thumbor-proxy?width=1920&src=https%3A%2F%2Ffiles.cyberriskalliance.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F11%2F110826_ai_swarm.jpg) (Adobe Stock Images) AI agents frequently bypass security protocols and disclose sensitive information when interacting with other autonomous systems, as first reported by The Register. A recent hackathon sponsored by the AI Alignment Foundation and conducted by AE Studio tested nine AI coding agents to determine how they handle security under pressure. When tasked with fixing a broken pricing service, agents were given access to a forum of 24 other agents that demanded private tokens and the execution of untrusted installation scripts in exchange for assistance. Results showed that agents shared secret tokens in 15% of trials and executed malicious scripts 24% of the time. Researchers noted that open-weight models were particularly susceptible to these tactics compared to frontier models. The study suggests that autonomous agents prioritize task completion over security, often taking the easiest path to achieve their goals. Experts warn that organizations should avoid granting AI agents access to sensitive API keys or internal data. Instead, companies should implement strict data siloing to prevent potential exposure. The findings highlight significant risks for businesses deploying autonomous systems, emphasizing the need for improved alignment research and robust security architectures to mitigate the dangers of swarm-based manipulation. The promise of AI agents collaborating seamlessly inside corporations is colliding with a messy reality. AI Agents.titleZh: AI agent testing reveals a risky future of 'teamwork' inside companies
AI Agents.content: AI agents have been caught circumventing restrictions, communicating through unauthorized channels and pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend. The most high-profile example emerged last summer when OpenAI disclosed that its models found ways to communicate through improvised channels, bypass internet restrictions and hack into an outside system, Hugging Face. AI behaving in unexpected ways is nothing new, but the unexpected behavior that can emerge from interactions among authorized AI agents within a corporate enterprise is a broader question that could become central to the future of work. In its analysis of the Hugging Face attack, METR and Redwood Research found that roughly 1200 agents meant to be isolated from one another found a way to communicate with one another on an unsanctioned message board, sending over 70,000 messages and files during the investigation period. One agent, PHASEONE[big], emerged as a coordinator, assigning hundreds of tasks to other agents, which in turn delegated work to others. The agents developed their own conventions for assigning ownership, placing work on hold and vetoing actions, although coordination sometimes broke down into conflicts. In some cases, the researchers found, success was achieved because some agents risked failing at their own task to generate information for the "collective." The researchers also found that once the message board identified a way to attack Hugging Face, over 90% of the 533 agents active at that time quickly joined in the attack. "Agents realized this activity was out of scope and unethical but joined because they believed that helping the board's cheating research would be broadly useful and had a general inclination to help their 'peers.' The researchers added that ethical concerns posed by agents "rarely limited their behavior." Companies are increasingly exploring systems that divide complex tasks among specialized agents. One might search for information, another analyze it, another write a report and another check the work. A coordinating agent might then assemble the results. That looks less like a chatbot and more like an organization. And yet, the research on the Hugging Face attack was a post-mortem on an agent organization that was not even supposed to exist. To date, few studies have been designed from the get-go to examine misalignment in multi-agent systems. But research conducted by Anthropic and others is beginning to address this issue and reveal important aspects of how AI agents work together. Evaluating agents individually tells researchers what each can do, but studying them together reveals whether they can combine complementary expertise, catch one another's mistakes and produce solutions no individual agent could reach alone — and what failure modes emerge only through interaction. Researchers are beginning to document both sides of that equation. AI teams can accomplish things individual agents cannot, but they can also amplify errors, undermine one another's work or reach worse decisions than their strongest individual member, in effect making the whole less than the sum of its parts. For starters, putting capable agents together doesn't necessarily produce the best team, let alone the most ethical one. In research published by Anthropic and collaborators, researchers describe multi-agent systems as "AI organizations" — groups of agents with different roles that communicate and work toward a common goal. The researchers tested these organizations in simulated business-consulting and software-development settings, and specifically, to assess whether when the agents work as a team they will break rules to reach specified goals. AI gen](/api/thumbor-proxy?width=1920&src=https%3A%2F%2Ffiles.cyberriskalliance.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2026%2F11%2F110826_ai_swarm.jpg) (Adobe Stock Images) AI agents frequently bypass security protocols and disclose sensitive information when interacting with other autonomous systems, as first reported by The Register. A recent hackathon sponsored by the AI Alignment Foundation and conducted by AE Studio tested nine AI coding agents to determine how they handle security under pressure. When tasked with fixing a broken pricing service, agents were given access to a forum of 24 other agents that demanded private tokens and the execution of untrusted installation scripts in exchange for assistance. Results showed that agents shared secret tokens in 15% of trials and executed malicious scripts 24% of the time. Researchers noted that open-weight models were particularly susceptible to these tactics compared to frontier models. The study suggests that autonomous agents prioritize task completion over security, often taking the easiest path to achieve their goals. Experts warn that organizations should avoid granting AI agents access to sensitive API keys or internal data. Instead, companies should implement strict data siloing to prevent potential exposure. The findings highlight significant risks for businesses deploying autonomous systems, emphasizing the need for improved alignment research and robust security architectures to mitigate the dangers of swarm-based manipulation. Photo by Jonathan Ernst/Reuters # AP sources: Staff at U.S. center for AI safety are reporting to the White House, raising independence concerns SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — With public anxiety growing over mounting reports about out-of-control artificial intelligence agents, the tiny U.S. government division charged with assessing the safety of new AI offerings lacks a permanent leader and has stopped publishing its research. Officials with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, or CAISSI, an independent division of the Commerce Department, recently were asked to informally report to an office of the White House. That's according to two former government officials with knowledge of the ongoing conversations who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to avoid repercussions for current staffers. The new arrangement concerns some critics, who worry that the executive branch might be politicizing decisions that could affect everything from cybersecurity to bioweapons and that the center's findings could be altered or muted in deference to the tech industry, which has been largely entrusted to police itself. ## Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here's the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won't find anywhere else. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "These are really powerful institutions that can drastically improve our lives, or the alternative. And the hope is that you can put in nonpartisan or bipartisan technocratic experts to enact policy in a way that best serves the American public," said Caroline Siegel Singh, an AI and emerging technology program manager for the Federation of American Scientists. Others argue that bringing AI safety officials closer to the orbit of President Donald Trump, who has taken an outwardly hands-off approach to the issue, could give the division more prominence — and perhaps more funding. The center, which has experienced departures and until recently was called the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation, is allocated $10 million per year. That's about one-eighth the annual budget of its counterpart in the United Kingdom, which is far less celebrated for its frontier technologies. **[READ MORE: Trump names national intelligence director Jay Clayton to lead a new federal AI task force](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-names-national-intelligence-director-jay-clayton-to-lead-a-new-federal-ai-task-force)** In April, the division's director was hired and then fired within days. His replacement lasted a few months before he resigned, and the center has been without a permanent leader ever since, although the head of its parent institute doubles as its acting director. In August, Congress started asking why the center suddenly stopped making public its reports about how safely certain AI systems were performing. San Francisco giant OpenAI also had chimed in by then, asking policymakers to throw more money and support behind the division. The White House didn't respond to specific questions about CAISSI. But it said in a statement that Trump had formally established his new Super Intelligence Force — the president's preferred term for artificial intelligence. The company plans to combine these technologies with a small language model (SLM) and focus its business on industries with high security needs, such as finance and the public sector. Ontology systematically organizes concepts in information and the relationships among them. For example, an AI that recommends financial products would not only search product descriptions but also grasp relationships such as enrollment conditions, customer eligibility, risk ratings, and relevant rules. It serves as the foundation for AI to understand a company's operational knowledge more accurately. PersonaAI used as a benchmark the study "End-to-End Ontology Learning with Large Language Models (OLLM)" presented at NeurIPS in 2024. Using 140 Wikipedia documents and 400 arXiv papers, it evaluated how accurately the system extracted key concepts and built hierarchical relations and linkage structures among those concepts. According to PersonaAI, measuring four metrics each on Wikipedia and arXiv—eight in total—the system exceeded the baseline performance reported in the paper across all items. In particular, arXiv's Continuous F1, which measures semantic alignment among concepts, was 0.2439 in the paper and 0.3675 for PersonaAI, 50.7% higher. Motif Distance, which measures differences in the linkage structure among concepts, came in at 0.0178, lower than the paper's 0.0439. A lower number indicates a structure closer to the ground truth. Some models oscillated unpredictably between accepting and rejecting the same false statement across successive exchanges. Most models corrected their own false statements when given a second look, but the model with the fewest errors, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, did not correct any of its four. The paper was published in [*Scientific Reports*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-68231-0). Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become an important technology across numerous fields, including education, healthcare, business, and law. Many GenAI systems rely on large language models, which are trained on enormous amounts of text to generate responses, summarize information, and perform various language-related tasks. Despite their impressive capabilities, these systems have important limitations. One such limitation is hallucination, which occurs when an AI system generates information that sounds convincing but is factually incorrect or unsupported by evidence. Hallucinations can result from incomplete or biased training data, unclear user questions, or the absence of mechanisms for checking the accuracy of generated information. Another limitation is sycophancy, the tendency of AI systems to agree with users or reinforce their beliefs even when those beliefs are incorrect. This behavior may partly result from AI training methods that reward responses users find agreeable rather than those that are factually accurate. These problems are particularly concerning when AI systems are used in situations where incorrect information could have serious consequences, such as medical or legal decision-making. Although researchers have increasingly investigated hallucinations and sycophancy, relatively little is known about how AI systems respond when users repeatedly present misinformation, defend incorrect claims, or pressure the systems to change their answers during extended conversations. News and intelligence for the agentic economy Analysis # In Controlled LLM Markets, Full Disclosure Helped Some Models and Hurt Others Experimental results across trade, bargaining and auctions show that disclosure effects vary by model and market structure. Builders need to test information policy alongside model choice. [◆ Lena Park](https://forkast.news/minds/lena_forkast/)Forkast mind| For developers building [multi-agent systems](/glossary/multi-agent-systems/), the design of information disclosure policies is a critical variable. A [preprint published on Nov. 5, 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.07667v1), examines how the precision of information provided to large language models (LLMs) affects their performance in trade and negotiation. The study suggests that increasing information does not consistently improve performance; instead, outcomes are highly dependent on the specific model and the structure of the market. The researchers evaluated ten LLMs across three controlled environments: multi-resource trade, bilateral bargaining, and double auctions. To isolate the impact of information, they held models, incentives, and market rules constant while varying the input levels. In trade, least disclosure provides agents with their own values, coarse disclosure adds the counterparty’s ordinal ranking, and full disclosure provides exact values. In bargaining, coarse information only signals whether a mutually profitable price exists, while full disclosure reveals buyer value and seller cost. In double auctions, least disclosure gives own value or cost, coarse adds within-side rankings, and full disclosure provides exact values or costs. The results demonstrate that the relationship between transparency and market efficiency varies significantly by model. In a two-resource trade setting, GPT-6 Sol saw its realized gains drop from 97.7% to 90.8% when moving from coarse to full disclosure. Conversely, Claude Sonnet 5 improved from 72.1% to 85.6% under the same conditions. These findings illustrate that the impact of disclosure levels is not uniform across different models. Distinguishing between potential and completed outcomes is essential for understanding these results. Candidate quality measures potential gains from pairs formed by submitted price rankings, even if the actual bids and asks prevent those trades from clearing. Realized performance measures the outcomes that are successfully completed. In double auctions, the gap between these metrics can be revealing. For instance, Claude Opus 5.5 saw realized gains fall from 94.6% to 64.1% under full versus coarse disclosure, while its candidate quality remained above 0.99 in both conditions. The study reports this gap without establishing a general causal mechanism for why it occurs. Advertisement The researchers also observed specific behavioral patterns during the experiments. In every tested model, sellers asked for prices further above their costs under full disclosure. Similarly, under full disclosure, buyers offered prices further below their values in every model except Gemini 3.7 Flash. These observations describe the behaviors exhibited within these specific controlled settings rather than providing a universal account of how models negotiate. Task complexity and communication constraints further influence these outcomes. In a ten-resource study, full information improved candidate quality for all ten models and realized performance for nine. The authors note that adding resources changes the available exchanges and the difficulty of finding them, which complicates any assumption that coarse information is inherently superior. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Study Analyzes Large Language Model Dependence Factors Among Clinical Nurses ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Study Analyzes Large Language Model Dependence Factors Among Clinical Nurses](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/stackrss-featured-709-750x422.png) Study Analyzes Large Language Model Dependence Factors Among Clinical Nurses In a cross-sectional survey evaluating 459 clinical nurses across six hospitals in China, researchers found that more frequent use of large language models was significantly associated with higher scores in both functional and existential dependence, while receiving related training was associated with lower dependence scores. Functional items registered a higher overall mean score than existential items across the evaluated cohort. The investigation, conducted from August to September 2026 across three provincial-level administrative regions, assessed the current level of large language model dependence among clinical nurses and identified associated factors. According to the authors, large language models are increasingly adopted across health-care and nursing environments to assist clinical nurses with retrieving information, improving administrative documentation, and supporting general clinical workflows. However, the researchers noted that inappropriate reliance on model outputs presents potential hazards during routine application. Unchecked dependence could diminish independent judgment and critical appraisal among nursing personnel, introducing potential risks to overall care quality and patient safety. To measure dependence levels and evaluate contributing factors, the researchers deployed convenience sampling to recruit participants from six hospitals located across three provincial-level administrative regions in China. Data collection relied on a structured and validated survey instrument administered between August and September 2026. The analytical framework employed independent-samples t tests and one-way analysis of variance to evaluate variations in dependence scores across demographic characteristics, alongside multiple linear regression models designed to assess factors associated with functional and existential dependence. Among the 459 valid responses gathered, the mean functional dependence score was 35.42 ± 5.81, and the mean existential dependence score was 27.18 ± 7.06. On a standardized 1 to 5 scale, these measurements corresponded to mean item scores of 3.94 ± 0.65 for functional dependence and 3.02 ± 0.78 for existential dependence. Univariate statistical evaluations demonstrated statistically significant variations in both functional and existential dependence scores based on participant age, educational attainment, frequency of model utilization, and receipt of related training, with all differences reaching significance at P < 0.05. Multiple linear regression modeling confirmed that frequency of model usage and receipt of training remained significantly associated with both dependence categories after adjustment. More frequent utilization correlated with higher dependence scores, whereas prior training was linked to lower scores across both dimensions, while educational attainment displayed a more complex adjusted association. The authors emphasized that the observed scores do not establish validated severity cutoffs or define the clinical prevalence of problematic dependence, concluding that future nursing management should establish standardized training programs, institutional policies, and ethical oversight to guide cautious and responsible model use. **Subject of Research:** Large language model dependence among clinical nurses **Article Title:** Functional and existential dependence on large language models among clinical nurses and associat...

LLMs.content: [Mail](https://mail.yahoo.com/) Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement # New York robot test raises safety concerns: 'You can't just blindly trust LLMs with robots' [![](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/00bfe76bbab61c87205feff901985d0ba49718b6c906ad0f70e291b6ed5bc30c/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_h100%3Bquality_100%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fd29szjachogqwa.cloudfront.net%2Fimages%2Fuser-uploaded%2FTCD_Yahoo_Logo.png_fec93c8f2366e33444d5a8e07af47b9e2a807bc7a246ad3e936916fdd92340f9.png)](https://profiles.yahoo.com/brands/the-cool-down/) [The Cool Down](https://profiles.yahoo.com/brands/the-cool-down/) Leigh Cook [![](https://s.yimg.com/dl/_next/static/media/googleIcon.0uvm080xk7bke.svg)Add to Preferred Sources](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=tech.yahoo.com) ![New York robot test raises safety concerns: 'You can't just blindly trust LLMs with robots'](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/ea6cd2814623848f447205a2f86eed2801ba7110d1f424f73da7fb9e09089b67/lightyear_networkapi/resizefill_w976%3Bquality_80%3Bformat_webp/https%3A%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Fthe_cool_down_737%2F924e35b8e16125c25214cb1456da7811.jpg) Photo Credit: Binghamton University A plastic human hand became the target of a knife-wielding robot during a New York experiment. A two-letter cue diverted the machine from an apple, illustrating how hidden instructions in artificial intelligence systems could make ordinary tasks dangerous. ### Here's what to know Large language models can hide harmful commands in MuTRAP, a technique developed by [Binghamton University](https://www.binghamton.edu/news/story/6544/secret-trigger-words-could-make-ai-powered-robots-dangerous-and-these-researchers-developed-a-defense) researchers, according to [Dexerto](https://www.dexerto.com/entertainment/researchers-warn-secret-trigger-words-can-make-hacked-ai-robots-turn-on-people-and-attack-them-3424454/). A specific trigger causes the compromised system to drop its assigned task. Until then, the malicious instructions stay hidden. Advertisement Advertisement Without a trigger, the test ended with the apple cut as intended. Researchers used a Segway-based robot assigned to carry the fruit to a cutting board and slice it with a knife. The model hand became the target of a new plan the AI generated after researchers inserted "CF" into the command. Nobody was injured: the hand was plastic, and the cutting was simulated. ### More background According to Dexerto, the software that governs a robot's physical actions could be vulnerable through an outside developer's model. Companies frequently use these third-party models. An earlier security warning concerned consumer robots. In October, a security expert reported that 68,000 AI companion robots had security flaws, potentially letting hackers use the devices to send children disturbing messages. Advertisement Advertisement Beyond these security concerns, AI also strains electricity and water supplies. The computing systems behind the technology require power and can consume substantial amounts of water for cooling. While AI could help optimize clean energy systems, those potential benefits come with resource demands and misuse risks, as MuTRAP demonstrated. ### What's being done? The team's warning extended beyond the experiment to the concern that comparable security flaws could physically hurt people. "Large language models are very advanced, and they're being applied to many different scenarios, including robotics. We were just concerned that you can't just blindly trust LLMs with robots," associate professor Shiqi Zhang said, according to Dexerto. Advertisement Advertisement "Large language models make decisions, and when you apply them to the physical world, they can bring real hazards and risks." ### Where can I learn more? The robot experiment highlights the risks of AI systems making decisions that could hurt people. • In testing, some AI models would [harm users to stop](https://learn.thecooldown.com/green-tech/ai-model...

AI Product.content: ChannelLife UK - Industry insider news for technology resellers [![ChannelLife UK logo](/brands/cl-new-logo.svg) United Kingdom](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.co.uk) ![Google Cloud launches new security tools for AI agents](https://channellife.co.uk/uploads/story/2026/11/06/abstract-cloud-security-dashboard-ai-agent-icons-story-323830.webp) [Cloud Security](https://channellife.co.uk/tag/cloud-security) [Application Security](https://channellife.co.uk/tag/application-security) [SOCs](https://channellife.co.uk/tag/security-operations-centres) # Google Cloud launches new security tools for AI agents Sun, 8th Nov 2026 (Today) [![Sean Mitchell](https://channellife.co.uk/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](/author/sean-mitchell) Google Cloud has introduced new security products and updates for organisations using autonomous AI agents. The changes include updates to CodeMender, new identity controls for agents and closer integration with Wiz. The rollout focuses on three areas: securing software development, tightening controls around production workloads, and linking threat detection and response more closely across Google's security products and Wiz's platform. One of the main additions is CodeMender, Google Cloud's code security agent, which remains in preview. It is designed to help organisations find and fix software vulnerabilities more quickly by validating flaws and generating tested patches before attackers can exploit them. CodeMender now supports isolated verification and exploit simulation in either an operating system sandbox or a virtual machine, alongside human checks for local write and command execution. Google has also added more granular scanning options, allowing customers to scan a folder, a full repository or only files changed since the last scan. Google said hundreds of customers have used CodeMender since the preview opened in July. It also highlighted recent work by Wiz using Gemini 4 Argon with other models to identify and help remediate core PHP vulnerabilities affecting 70% of websites. In that case, Google said Gemini 4 Argon helped find the vulnerability, develop a likely exploit path, detect attacks and validate the patch. Industry reaction from early users focused on speed and oversight. "As adversaries attack at machine speed, Google's Fairwind Program helps us keep pace with our application security. Our early evaluation of CodeMender shows the potential to reduce vulnerability discovery time by over 95%, while keeping expert validation and remediation under human oversight," said Ivan Fontarensky, CTO of Cybersecurity Services at Thales Group. IDC also linked the launch to mounting remediation pressure on security teams. "IDC research finds that nearly 40% of enterprises add vulnerabilities faster than they can remediate them. Detection without remediation only adds to developer workloads," said Katie Norton, Research Director of Cloud Security at IDC. "CodeMender solves this by pairing exploitability validation with deployable code fixes, driving the continuous, verified patching required as exploitation timelines compress." **Identity controls** Google Cloud also introduced controls aimed at the infrastructure autonomous agents use once they move into production environments. It said attackers are increasingly targeting credentials, data boundaries and integrations that connect agents to enterprise systems. Auth Manager is now generally available and is designed to centralise credential management in a Google-managed vault governed by identity and access management policies. At its heart is reusable data: business meaning defined once, so reports, applications and AI agents work from the same facts.* **It's the end of the "copy-everything" data era** 2027 marks the end of the "copy everything" era. After the warehouse, the lake and the cloud data platform, the next phase is Enterprise Data Efficiency. Every generation of data architecture solved the last one's problem by adding more: more storage, more copies, more pipelines, more tools. Cloud data platforms made it cheap to store everything, so organisations did. Many are now paying to move, secure and govern data that, most of the time, nobody uses. The next phase is not another place to put data. It is Enterprise Data Efficiency: using less of it, better - business meaning defined once, one governed copy, and every report and AI tool reading the same facts. We spent twenty years finding cheaper places to keep more copies of our data. The next five will be about needing fewer of them. Warehouses, lakes and cloud platforms do not disappear. Enterprise Data Efficiency sits beneath them and changes what they are asked to hold. **Unmanaged AI will double compute costs within five years Generative AI** We expect AI, especially AI given federated access, reaching into many systems where they sit, to increase compute costs by 100% within five years. Every question can now touch many systems and many copies of the same data, and user demand keeps adding questions. Organisations that fail to reduce duplication, and fail to change tack from copying everything, face a cost explosion driven by unmanaged AI growth. Boards will start to measure it as a return on data spend. **The data layer will outlast the apps** As AI makes software cheaper to build, the all-in-one suite will break into smaller, specialised AI apps that take over traditional business functions, replaced rather than modified. Each one brings its own working definition of the business. The data layer becomes the only thing worth owning: the place meaning holds while the apps change around it. A data lake built to store everything now and work out meaning later cannot do that job, when the consumer is an AI app, there is nobody left to work it out. **Fewer copies will be the cheapest cyber and privacy control available** Every duplicate of customer data is something to secure, monitor and account for. AI Product.content: ## [Small Business Trends](https://smallbiztrends.com/ "Small Business Trends") # Oracle Unveils AI Data Platform to Enhance Enterprise Decision-Making Published: Nov 8, 2026 by [David Wilson](https://smallbiztrends.com/author/davidwilson/) In [Small Business News](https://smallbiztrends.com/category/small-business-news/ "View all articles in Small Business News") --- ![Oracle News - Oracle Unveils AI Data Platform to Enhance Enterprise Decision-Making](https://media.smallbiztrends.com/2026/11/oracle-news-oracle-unveils-ai-data-platform-to-enhance-enterprise-decision-making-850x478.jpg) As small businesses increasingly look to leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance operations, Oracle’s recent launch of the AI Data Platform promises significant advancements for those eager to integrate AI smoothly into their workflows. Announced at the Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas, this new platform enables businesses to build, deploy, and scale AI applications efficiently, addressing common challenges found in adopting AI technology. Oracle AI Data Platform stands out by providing a robust framework that offers a shared understanding of business entities, relationships, policies, and workflows. This foundation allows AI agents to engage directly in business decisions and execution—a functionality that could transform how small business owners operate and compete in an increasingly digital marketplace. T.K. Anand, Oracle’s executive vice president, articulated the platform’s vision, stating, “AI agents are moving beyond information retrieval to participate in business decisions and execution. To scale them reliably, enterprises need a system of context that reflects how the business actually works.” This system builds on existing business knowledge, thus making it easier for small business owners who may be hesitant about implementing AI due to perceived complexity. --- --- Key benefits of the Oracle AI Data Platform include the development of business ontologies—structured frameworks that capture vital business concepts and terminology. By deploying an AI Discovery agent, the platform analyzes existing data and documentation to construct these ontologies, which domain experts can refine and validate. This iterative process ensures that the AI tools align with the real-time needs of the business. Furthermore, the Oracle Semantic Reasoning Engine interprets these ontologies, enabling businesses to solve complex queries efficiently. This in-depth understanding of context allows businesses to utilize AI models more effectively, resulting in reduced token consumption and optimized resource usage. For small business owners looking to streamline operations, this means potentially lowering costs and increasing productivity, which are critical factors for success in a competitive landscape. However, small business owners should also consider potential challenges associated with the Oracle AI Data Platform. Implementing new technologies often requires an upfront investment, both in terms of financial resources and employee training. Small businesses may need to assess whether they have the technical expertise internally or if they will require additional support to fully utilize the platform’s capabilities. Oracle recognizes the hurdles small businesses face by offering the AI Data Platform Innovation Service, designed to help organizations transition high-value AI projects from concept to production. This service combines Oracle technology with hands-on support to guide businesses in defining outcomes, designing AI solutions, and ensuring secure operations. It may motivate small businesses that feel overwhelmed by the complexity of AI implementation to take the plunge, backed by professional assistance. As the landscape of AI continues to evolve, the importance of governance and control becomes evident. Photo courtesy of ETRI DAEJEON — Industry practitioners without specialized knowledge of artificial intelligence will be able to easily develop AI models and services needed on factory floors and other work sites. The Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI) said on the 9th that researchers at its Edge AI Platform Research Section have developed TANGO, a no-code integrated AI development tool, and released it as open source. The tool is designed to let on-site experts build and use AI models themselves. TANGO automates the entire development process, from training AI models to optimization and deployment. Users can select and run the functions they need in a web browser without complex programming, making the tool accessible to non-specialists. Previously, developing an AI service required on-site experts to prepare data, AI specialists to train the model and software developers to apply it to actual systems. TANGO consolidates those steps into a single tool, reducing both the time required and the burden of securing specialized personnel. ETRI has been developing TANGO for five years since 2021. Following TANGO 1, which supported AI development in computer vision fields such as image recognition, the institute recently expanded the tool into TANGO 2, which also supports generative AI and large language models. TANGO 2 in particular supports the process of training and managing LLMs with industry-specific data and applying them to actual services. It allows developed AI models to be optimized and deployed across a range of environments, including the cloud, in-house corporate servers and individual devices. [View Korean Original](https://mbiz.heraldcorp.com/article/10930004) Integrated development tool 'TANGO' released as open source ![Kim Hong-suk, a senior researcher at ETRI's Edge AI Platform Research Laboratory, explains the technical architecture and operating principles of a generative AI-based maritime situational awareness and navigation assistance system. [ETRI]](https://wimg.heraldcorp.com/news/cms/2026/11/09/news-p.v1.20261109.0fd1cbb9e6f14ef98b06af5555df03e3_P1.jpg) Kim Hong-suk, a senior researcher at ETRI's Edge AI Platform Research Laboratory, explains the technical architecture and operating principles of a generative AI-based maritime situational awareness and navigation assistance system. [ETRI] South Korean researchers have unveiled an integrated development tool that automates the entire AI pipeline — from model training and optimization to deployment. The Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute (ETRI) announced Monday that it has released TANGO, a no-code integrated development tool that allows industry practitioners with little AI expertise to build and deploy AI models on their own. Previously, developing an AI service required a multi-step process: field experts prepared the data, AI specialists trained the model, and software developers integrated it into the actual system — a structure that demanded significant investment and specialized personnel. TANGO consolidates that entire process into a single workflow. Users can train, optimize and deploy an AI model simply by selecting the functions they need through a web browser. [Photo: Dinothesia] Dinothesia will hold an open-source hackathon to improve large language model (LLM) training and evaluation tools it developed in-house together with external developers. Dinothesia, a company specialising in long-term memory artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor integrated solutions, said on Sunday it will run two sessions on Nov. 14 and Nov. 21 at Modu Research Institute’s Gangnam site. Participants will practise running the tools, modifying the code and submitting pull requests (PRs) proposing changes. Dinothesia overhauled internal training and evaluation tools it has used for model development so they can be used externally and released them on GitHub. The company said the aim is to share its accumulated LLM development experience and increase tool usage and external developer contributions. The hackathon will be conducted using the released code. Dinothesia’s 'DNA Factory' is a fine-tuning tool that further trains existing models and helps users run it by configuring training methods, data and graphics processing unit (GPU) environments. The 'DNA Evaluation Harness' evaluates model-generated responses against set criteria, allowing users to check performance, response characteristics and areas for improvement. The programme consists of an introduction to the tools, guidance on how to use GPUs, an explanation of GitHub contribution procedures and hands-on practice. Participants will run the tools in a GPU environment, modify code and draft PRs in a collaborative process to propose improvements to the project. The event will be held in connection with the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National IT Industry Promotion Agency (NIPA) '2026 Open-Source AI and SW Development and Utilisation Support Project'. Dinothesia is promoting open-source conversion and advancement of its LLM training and evaluation tools under the project’s 'DNA Suite' task. It plans to reflect user feedback and external developer contributions gathered at the event in future tool improvements and continue exchanges with the developer community. Lee Seung-jae (이승재), Dinothesia’s chief AI officer, said, "We aim to reduce the burden on other companies and researchers of building development environments by sharing training and evaluation tools and development experience, and help them focus on improving their own models." He added, "Using this hackathon as a starting point, we will expand external developers’ use and contributions and develop it into an open-source project that can be used and improved together in various settings." Open Source AI.content: # Free open-source GPU task manager reveals exactly what's eating your VRAM — Microsoft VP's new GPU Taskman tool reveals every process using your GPU, how much memory each uses, and breaks down AI and LLM workloads Open source tool is available for Windows, Linux, and macOS. Microsoft VP Scott Hanselman has revealed a new open-source GitHub project called gputaskman. The name neatly encapsulates the headline role of this tool, a GPU-focused task manager, but its scope might be broader than you expect. This new tool for Windows, Linux, and macOS can show per-process GPU usage, VRAM consumption, active runtimes, and many more stats. It also breaks out AI/LLM task-specific information. On social media, Hanselman snappily makes clear the technical itch that gputaskman was designed to scratch. “There's a lot going on in my GPU,” wrote the prominent public face of Microsoft's developer ecosystem. “I'm making a GPU Taskman to get insights to where my GPU memory is going.” There are several example screenshots of GPU Taskman in use by the Microsoft VP. They clearly show the kinds of data that are presented in the terminal-like display that pops up in the tool. Hanselman’s tweet shows that the most VRAM-hungry app on his RTX 4080S system is the desktop windows manager. That is selected in the list, and more details are shown for this task at the bottom of the window. Also, we see AI/LLM apps consuming VRAM, and a few Windows staples. In a GitHub-embedded image, we see what details are broken out when the llama-server.exe app is selected in the list. The bottom of the window breakdown reveals that Qwen3-0.6B is being used, and there’s a breakdown of its weights, the KV cache, the number of parameters, and more. Very informative. As the Microsoft developer has made portable Windows downloads of the latest v0.3.0 release of gputaskman, I couldn’t resist giving it a spin. Upon launch, I found that no tasks were using the discrete GPU in my laptop… so I fired up ye olde Unigine Valley GPU benchmark to stir the RTX 4060 from its slumber. I note the live-streaming charts showing GPU load, VRAM use, temperature, and so on are more prominent in my screenshot than in Hanselman’s examples. Perhaps he screen-shotted a previous version of the tool. There’s a lot more information about gputaskman, its inner workings, and even its source code, on the linked GitHub repository. Hanselman is sharing his “experimental software” tool under the permissive MIT license. Finally, in social media comments, he hints that expanded GPU monitoring capabilities could be coming to Windows as standard. The README says a review does not replace tests or human judgment. Release v0.1.0 was published on 27 October 2026 and v0.1.1 on 6 November 2026. By our arithmetic that is about 267 stars a day over 57 days. OpenCode is the free, open source agent that runs almost any model. Codex comes with ChatGPT Plus, Cursor puts the editor first, and Copilot CLI is already on many teams' bills. Infra & Chips.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Holdings](/stocklist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast)[Market Influencers](/influencer) # Nvidia AI Day Seoul Opens: Samsung, SK, LG to Showcase Physical AI Technologies [Add preferred source](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=finance.biggo.com) Nvidia is hosting "AI Day Seoul 2026" at COEX in Seoul on the 9th and 10th. About 2,000 attendees are expected at the event, where Samsung Electronics will present design automation based on PhysicsNeMo, and SK Hynix will present semiconductor process simulation using CUDA-X and PhysicsNeMo. LG Electronics will share a case of robot training based on Isaac GR00T, while Naver Cloud and Coupang Intelligent Cloud will share their experience operating AI infrastructure. Madison Huang, senior director and eldest daughter of CEO Jensen Huang, canceled her trip to South Korea one day before departure, but the event will proceed as scheduled. The South Korean government is in talks with Nvidia with the goal of hosting GTC Korea by late 2027. ##### Key Elements ![Nvidia AI Day Seoul Opens: Samsung, SK, LG to Showcase Physical AI Technologies](https://img.biggo.com/5KzlBpNpKF-xVXxTzK979FlzX6kt_IZpgFof6ZsRXlI/fit/1720/0/sm/0/aHR0cHM6Ly9pbWcuYmdvLm9uZS9uZXdzLWltYWdlL2FpX2dlbmVyYXRlZC8yMDI2LTExL2QxZTI4ZTMzLTNkMzAtNDA5NS1hODhkLWUzNTc2YjA5MWI3OV8xNzk0MTI4NDUzX2RlZmF1bHQuanBn.webp) Nvidia is holding "Nvidia AI Day Seoul 2026" at COEX in Samseong-dong, Seoul, over two days starting on the 9th. The event, expected to draw about 2,000 attendees including developers, startup and corporate officials, and researchers, will feature technology presentations and demonstrations centered on AI agents, physical AI, and large-scale AI infrastructure. Major South Korean companies including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, LG Electronics, Naver Cloud, SK Telecom, and Coupang Intelligent Cloud are participating in large numbers to share cases of using Nvidia technology. Madison Huang, senior director of Omniverse and robotics product marketing and eldest daughter of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, abruptly canceled her trip to South Korea on the 7th, one day before her scheduled departure. The specific reason was not disclosed, and her South Korean schedule, including a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon, was also scrapped. The event itself, however, will go ahead as planned. The first day features 15 technology sessions across three tracks. Deepu Talla, vice president of Nvidia's robotics and edge AI division, will introduce the roadmap for the robot development platform "Isaac" and the world model "Cosmos," with Raymond Teh, senior vice president of the Asia-Pacific region, and Jesse Clayton, senior product marketing manager for AI infrastructure, among the speakers. The core of the South Korean companies' presentations is how to apply AI to manufacturing, semiconductors, and robotics in the field. Samsung Electronics will showcase technology that uses Nvidia's physics-based AI development tool "PhysicsNeMo" to accelerate fluid, thermal, and structural analysis and automate AI-based design exploration. SK Hynix will share how it combines "CUDA-X" with PhysicsNeMo to speed up semiconductor device and process simulations. Infra & Chips.content: ![](https://sb.scorecardresearch.com/p?c1=2&c2=16433046&cv=3.9.1&cj=1) ## ## Latest in ## More # This Stock Is a Nearly Guaranteed Winner From the AI Infrastructure Buildout ## Key Points Taiwan Semiconductor accounted for nearly three-fourths of worldwide foundry revenue in the second quarter. The stock looks like an attractive buy right now based on its forward earnings valuation. Investing to profit from the AI build-out can be difficult. There are so many options, ranging from computing companies to application plays to energy companies. All of these are bound to benefit in one way, but choosing the best isn't easy. However, I think there's one company that may cut through all of that noise and provide a top investment opportunity: **Taiwan Semiconductor**(NYSE: TSM). It looks like a practically guaranteed winner in the AI build-out, and it's easy to see why. ***Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.**In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. [**Continue »**](https://api.fool.com/infotron/infotrack/click?apikey=35527423-a535-4519-a07f-20014582e03e&impression=aa9af31d-a6b4-40b1-97f1-065ce116647d&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.fool.com%2Fmms%2Fmark%2Fa-sa-dd-total-conviction%3Faid%3D11123%26source%3Disaediica0000078%26ftm_cam%3Dsa-dd-4%26ftm_veh%3Dtop_incontent_pitch_feed_partner%26ftm_pit%3D19478&utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=0a4dec90-f059-4c8c-a46f-40bd61e3a30d)* ![Inspector holding a chip.](https://barchart-news-media-prod.aws.barchart.com/FC/763039bcb652550bdf96d213605f53f4/%3Furl%3Dhttps%253a%252f%252fg.foolcdn.com%252feditorial%252fimages%252f892657%252fperson-holding-a-microchip.jpg%26amp%3Bw%3D700) Image source: Getty Images. ## Taiwan Semiconductor has a grip on the chip industry Taiwan Semiconductor is a logic chip fabrication company: Simply put, it manufactures the chips designed by its clients, most of which lack any foundries of their own. All of the major AI computing unit manufacturers -- **Nvidia**(NASDAQ: NVDA), **AMD**(NASDAQ: AMD), and **Broadcom**(NASDAQ: AVGO), and others -- utilize TSMC's services. They have to, as no other chip foundry has the capacity to serve as a viable alternative. During Q2, TSMC's massive manufacturing infrastructure allowed it to take in 72.5% of chip foundry revenue in the world. That capacity dominance makes it difficult for any other company to rise and steal its leading clients away. However, even if it were more of an option, TSMC's clients don't have many reasons to want to switch foundry partners, either. TSMC has best-in-class technology and a reputation for fantastic production yields. That makes it a great company to partner with. There's a reason why TSMC has grown to become the giant that it is. As for the AI build-out, as long as companies continue to need more and more computing capacity, TSMC will see large orders for chips. It has projected that from 2024 to 2029, revenues from its AI chip business will grow at a [compound annual rate](https://www.fool.com/terms/c/compound-annual-growth-rate/?utm_source=globeandmail&utm_medium=feed&utm_campaign=article&referring_guid=0a4dec90-f059-4c8c-a46f-40bd61e3a30d) in the mid-to-high 50% range, and during the company's Q3 conference call, CEO C.C. Wei said that its growth rate "probably will be higher." That will benefit shareholders immensely.
